tool.name: InvertRaster
tool.summary: Numerically inverts a raster -- each output cell is 1/(x + c) -- so a surface in which HIGH values mean good habitat (a land facet density raster, a diversity index) becomes a least-cost surface in which that good ground is CHEAP to cross. The small constant c (default 0.1) prevents zero cells from dividing to NoData. A multi-band Land Facet Density raster produces one single-band cost raster per facet, named from the density raster's own records, with the stored integer scaling converted back to 0-1 proportions first. A modernized port of the Land Facet Corridor Designer's Invert Raster tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHAT THIS TOOL DOES. Least-cost corridor tools read their input upside down from the way habitat surfaces are usually made: LOW cells are easy to cross and HIGH cells are barriers. The surfaces this tool family produces measure quality the other way -- more density of a land facet, more diversity of facets, the better. This tool bridges the two by taking the numeric reciprocal of every cell: each output value is 1 divided by (the input value plus a small constant). Ground where density or diversity is high comes out with low cost, and the result can be handed directly to CorridorDesigner or Cost Distance as a resistance surface.
THE CONSTANT. Dividing by a cell whose value is exactly zero is undefined, and such cells would become NoData holes in the cost surface -- holes that least-cost analysis treats as impassable. Adding a small constant to every cell before inverting removes the problem, and the Land Facet manual strongly recommends it, suggesting 0.1 (which makes the diversity resistance formula exactly 1/(H' + 0.1), as published). The default here is 0.1. Clear the constant only for a deliberate reason; the tool will warn, and any zero cells then become NoData just as the original did. The constant also caps the maximum cost: with c = 0.1 the worst possible cell (value 0) costs 10 and the best possible density cell (proportion 1.0) costs about 0.91, an 11-to-1 range.
WHAT THE ORIGINAL WAS FOR, AND WHAT THIS ONE ADDS. In the published workflow the Invert Raster tool exists to invert the Shannon's Index (diversity) raster into the cost surface for the facet-interspersion corridor; the individual facet corridors get their cost surfaces from the Mahalanobis tool instead, which already produces low-is-good values. This version serves that same purpose -- run it on a Diversity Indices output -- and adds direct support for inverting a Land Facet Density raster, for building corridors that simply follow a facet's abundance.
MULTI-BAND DENSITY INPUT: ONE COST RASTER PER FACET. The original inverted a single chosen band per run. A Land Facet Density raster holds one band per facet, and its inversions are terminal cost surfaces for tools that expect a single band -- so this tool writes ONE single-band raster per band in a single run, each named from the facet recorded in the density raster's metadata (for example "Inv_Valley_Cluster_2"). A single-band input simply produces one output raster named from the input.
STORED DENSITY VALUES ARE CONVERTED BACK TO PROPORTIONS FIRST. Land Facet Density rasters store their 0-1 proportions as integers scaled by 10,000. Adding 0.1 to a raw stored value of, say, 6923 would make the constant meaningless and the cost curve unrecognizable. When the input carries a density record, each band is divided back to true 0-1 proportions before the constant is added, so the published cost curve is reproduced exactly; the run messages report the conversion. Values above the stored maximum (possible when a geodatabase has dropped the NoData declaration on a multi-band raster) are treated as NoData with a warning.
NEGATIVE VALUES. The reciprocal of a negative number is negative, and least-cost tools reject negative costs. Density and diversity surfaces are never negative, but this tool will invert any raster, so if cells are still negative after the constant is added their inverted values are written as-is -- faithfully to the original -- and the tool warns with a count. If you see that warning, either the input is not a quality surface or the constant needs to be larger.
NODATA. Input NoData stays NoData in the output. Cells that become NoData through division by zero are counted and reported separately, so you can tell missing input from a zero-valued one.
REFERENCES. Land Facet Corridor Designer: Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010, "Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors," Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01422.x); Brost, B.M., and P. Beier. 2012, "Use of land facets to design linkages for climate change," Ecological Applications 22:87-103 (https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0213.1); Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013, "Land Facet Corridor Designer: Extension for ArcGIS," Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm). Corridor Designer tools: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007, "CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors" (http://corridordesign.org).

dialogReference.para: The raster to invert: a surface in which HIGH values mean good habitat, such as a Land Facet Density raster (multi-band, one facet per band) or a Diversity Indices / Shannon's Index raster. A multi-band density raster produces one single-band cost raster per facet; any other raster is inverted band for band. When the input carries a Land Facet Density record, stored integer values are converted back to 0-1 proportions before the constant is added.
Where the inverted raster(s) are written -- a folder or a geodatabase. A folder destination produces GeoTIFFs. One single-band raster is written per input band.

The leading part of each output name. For a density raster the facet label follows ("Inv_Valley_Cluster_2"); for other rasters the input name (and band number when multi-band) follows. Defaults to "Inv".

A small constant added to every cell before taking the reciprocal, preventing zero cells from dividing to NoData and capping the maximum cost. The default 0.1 is the Land Facet manual's strong recommendation and reproduces the published diversity resistance formula 1/(H' + 0.1). Clear it only deliberately; zero-valued cells then become NoData, and the tool warns.

Optionally restrict the run. When the input is a Land Facet Density raster the list offers each facet by identifier and label; for other multi-band rasters supply plain band numbers. Leave empty to invert every band, which is the normal choice.

scriptExample.title: Invert Raster example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Invert a whole density raster (one cost surface per facet), then a Shannon's/Diversity raster with the recommended constant, then two facets only. Pass None for the constant to add nothing (zero cells then become NoData).
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# One inverted cost raster per land facet, at the recommended constant arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "landfacets_Density.tif", r"C:\project\cost", "Inv", 0.1)
# The diversity corridor's cost surface: 1 / (H' + 0.1) arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "facets_EffNum_q1.tif", r"C:\project\cost", "Inv", 0.1)
# Only facets 3 and 7 arcpy.jenness.InvertRaster( "landfacets_Density.tif", r"C:\project\cost", "Inv", 0.1, "3;7")
